newsitem.title: USA: Americans celebrate annual pursuit of happiness.
newsitem.headline: Americans celebrate annual pursuit of happiness.

text.p: Hundreds of thousands of completely sober people flocked to Washington's Mall on Friday to celebrate U.S. Independence Day and the uniquely American "pursuit of happiness."

Unfazed by a crackdown on drunkenness that restricted alcohol consumption to a few designated areas where $3 beers were available, Americans in their capital city found plenty to celebrate on the 221st anniversary of separation from British colonial rule.

"I'm glad that George (Washington) and all the boys did a great job breaking away from the British, to be honest," Wilson Ray Jr., an operations analyst at the Goddard Space Flight Centre in Greenbelt, Maryland, said while listening to a gospel music concert.

Like many Americans, Ray was feeling some national pride over the Pathfinder mission that landed on Mars on Friday. Others made note of the booming U.S. economy or the country's tradition of religious and political freedom.
"This is a great place to come," Ray said of the Mall, a grassy stretch from Capitol Hill to the Lincoln Memorial. "I'm just feeling a little bit more of an American today."
The day's festivities were to end with a grand fireworks show.

The Declaration of Independence, which is largely a list of complaints against the madness of King George III, also enshrines "life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness" as inalienable rights, a twist from John Locke's premise that it was "life, liberty and property" we all deserve.
No one interviewed at the Mall felt the ban against getting drunk in public violated the right to pursue happiness.

"I'm sure (Thomas) Jefferson meant more than a beer and a barbecue, although maybe he liked a glass of wine," said Harry Edwards, an engineer from northern New Jersey. "I don't view the Founding Fathers as a bunch of stuffed shirts. They were real people."
But as Washington taxi driver Jason McBride pointed out, the Founding Fathers were also white male property owners -- the blessings of liberty came later for women, slaves and Indians.
"I still consider myself patriotic, but you got to face the facts," he said.
As for others left out, there are also the British, who lost a colony but later picked up a close foreign ally.
Robert Chatterton Dickson, the British Embassy spokesman in Washington, said diplomats here were likely to spend the day watching parades or visiting the beach like everybody else.

"We all recognise that since 1776 the United States has been independent. It's very hard to imagine that it's ever been otherwise," Chatterton Dickson said. "For us it's a way to celebrate the remarkable achievements of the United States. We certainly don't spend the day swimming in bitterness."
